newsitem.title: POLAND: Swedish PM brings aid pledge to flooded Poles.
newsitem.headline: Swedish PM brings aid pledge to flooded Poles.

text.p: Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson toured flood-devastated south-west Poland on Thursday, bringing heartbroken villagers a promise of speedy aid.

Persson drove with Poland's Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz through villages of the Lubsza district still drying out after a three-week deluge in which flood waters reached roof eaves and made whole communities uninhabitable.
In the village of Dobrzyn, the two toured a wrecked school and were ushered by a weeping mother into the nightmare of fungus and wreckage that had been her home.
In her muddy courtyard, they were surrounded by villagers clamouring to hear when or whether they would be rehoused.
"Sweden will help... this will be a lot," Cimoszewicz told the dozens of distraught people amid a swarm of mosquitoes.
"We will build houses for flood victims as fast as we can... by the onset of winter," he said, clutching a mud-encrusted book he found in a school-room.

The Swedish prime minister's press office said in a statement Stockholm would grant Poland 125 million crowns ($15 million) in flood aid for the environment, housing projects and industrial cooperation.
Cimoszewicz said that under one project Sweden would build up to 1,000 apartments for homeless flood victims.

"Especially in these communities, here where most houses were covered with water and were so heavily damaged, new ones must be built and we appreciate this (Swedish help) very much," Cimoszewicz said.
Persson kept silent as he listened to local people fling questions, pleas and reproaches at his Polish host.

As in most of the hundreds of communities hit last month by Poland's worst flood in centuries there is a sense of injustice or anger in Dobrzyn, where people feel neglected by authorities as they grapple with the loss of everything they owned.
Cimoszewicz told the villagers that his government had already announced it would build 1,000 houses for those made homeless in the disaster.
"That's a drop in the ocean," growled a villager.
The premier argued that the 1,000 already made half the reported cases of destroyed houses. He reminded that other flooded areas had problems such as smashed roads and bridges.
He reassured, sympathised, and listed social security and other support measures, but the crowd seemed unconvinced. Even as he drove off a clamour continued.
"Where is my little girl going to sleep? In a house full of dangerous fungus?" "What will happen to us when winter comes?"
The ex-communist Cimoszewicz, who faces general elections next month, has been energetically touring such areas promoting a race to rehouse victims before winter.
The opposition accuses him and the government of delay and incompetence at the outset of the floods that swamped more than 6,600 sq km (2,800 sq miles) of the country -- charges he rejects.
In the five villages through which the premiers drove, swamped by the River Oder several kilometres away, there was little interest in the elections but much misery.
Outside once-fine brick houses typical of the region, people set pathetic bonfires of their goods, furniture, and children's clothes, all too contaminated to salvage.
The stench was worsened by desert-like fields of wasted grain and potatoes turned to poisonous pulp.
People cleaning up their homes but forced to camp in schoolhouses or with relatives spoke matter-of-factly about their problems, then suddenly turned away to weep.
"This was a beautiful village. It won awards," said Jozefa Fialka, 55, in the village Blota, whose name meaning mud has become horribly appropriate. "Now nobody will want to come here," she said.
